A Beginner's Guide to Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) Requests

The FOIA is a powerful tool for accessing federal government records. Learn how to draft, submit, and track an effective request.

Key takeaways

  • ✓FOIA covers federal executive agencies. States have their own public records laws.
  • ✓Specific requests get answered faster than broad ones.
  • ✓If a request is denied, the agency must explain how to appeal.

What is the Freedom of Information Act?

Enacted in 1967, the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) is a foundational federal law that gives you the legal right to request access to records from any federal agency. It is a vital tool for journalists, academic researchers, watchdog organizations, and engaged citizens seeking government transparency and accountability. The core presumption of FOIA is that government records belong to the public, and agencies must disclose them unless they fall under specific, legally defined exemptions.

What Can You Legally Request?

You can request a wide variety of documents, including internal emails, policy memos, statistical reports, meeting minutes, and datasets held by federal agencies (e.g., the FBI, EPA, FDA, or Department of Defense). However, the law includes nine specific exemptions to protect sensitive information. You cannot successfully request classified national defense information, confidential commercial or trade secret data, personal privacy records (like medical files), or active law enforcement investigatory files that could interfere with an ongoing case.

How to Submit a Successful FOIA Request

Drafting a successful FOIA request requires precision and patience. Follow these best practices:

  • Identify the Correct Agency: Determine which specific federal department or agency is most likely to hold the records you seek. Sending a request to the wrong agency will result in delays or a "no records found" response.
  • Be Highly Specific: Vague, overly broad requests (e.g., "all emails about climate change") are often rejected, delayed, or hit with massive fee estimates. Include specific dates, names of individuals, precise document types, and clear subject matter to help the agency's FOIA officers locate the files efficiently.
  • Submit Through Official Channels: Most major agencies now have dedicated online FOIA request portals (like FOIA.gov), which allow you to track the status of your request in real time. Alternatively, you can submit your request via certified mail.
  • Prepare for Fees and Delays: Agencies are allowed to charge reasonable search and duplication fees. However, fee waivers or reductions are often available for journalists, educators, and academic researchers whose work serves the public interest. Be prepared for a wait; complex requests can take months to process.

State-Level Equivalents: "Sunshine Laws"

It is crucial to remember that the federal FOIA only applies to federal executive branch agencies. It does not apply to Congress, the federal courts, or state and local governments. Each individual state has its own equivalent law, often called a "Sunshine Law" or Public Records Act, for accessing state, county, and city government documents. The processes, exemptions, and response times for these state-level requests vary significantly.

Writing a Request That Gets Results

Vague requests are slow and often rejected. Name the agency, the type of record, and a date range. Compare these two requests:

  • Weak: "All records about the highway project."
  • Stronger: "Copies of the signed construction contract, change orders, and final invoices for the Route 9 resurfacing project awarded in 2024, held by the Department of Transportation."

Include your contact details, say whether you prefer electronic delivery, and cite the law you are using. If you are not sure which office holds the record, many agencies have a FOIA public liaison who can point you in the right direction.

Timing, Fees, and Tracking

Federal agencies are generally required to respond to a FOIA request within 20 business days, although extensions for unusual circumstances and large backlogs are common. Most agencies assign a tracking number, so keep it and check status online or by email. Fees depend on who you are: commercial requesters pay search, review, and copying costs, while news media, educational, and noncommercial scientific requesters generally pay only for copying. You can also ask for a fee waiver if disclosure is in the public interest. Many agencies post their fee schedules online.

If Your Request Is Denied or Delayed

Agencies may withhold information that falls under one of nine statutory exemptions, such as certain national security, personal privacy, and law enforcement material. Even when an exemption applies, the agency is supposed to release the parts that can be separated. A denial letter must explain your right to appeal. A common deadline for an administrative appeal is at least 90 days after the denial, but check your letter for the exact date. The Office of Government Information Services (OGIS) offers free mediation of FOIA disputes, and requesters can also take a dispute to federal court.

Federal vs. State Requests

FOIA covers federal executive branch agencies. It does not apply to Congress, federal courts, or state and local governments. For records held by a city, county, school district, or state agency, you need that state's own public records law, which has its own name, deadlines, fees, and exemptions. State attorney general offices or open-government organizations often publish plain-language guides and sample request letters.
